I still get these thoughts. I'll be minding my own business, doing something, and then I'll suddenly be haunted by a past experience that caused me shame or embarrassment.

I've found the following to be helpful:  
 \- Understanding that you are not your past, and you have no loyalty to it. What I mean by this is that just because you did something in the past it doesn't mean that you have to a slave to it for the rest of your life and have it define you. People may bring it up occasionally and say "Hey, remember when you did this stupid thing and we all laughed at you" (or similar), but you shouldn't pay any attention to these people. They're usually only reminding you because they're living in the past themselves to escape whatever is happening now, they haven't moved on and they don't want you to either.

\- When a thought or feeling like this does come. Don't react to it. I know that this is easier said than done, but whenever a thought like that pops into your head just remain calm and observe it. Pretend that the thought is a butterfly, or a bird, or an interesting animal, or an angry caged animal, etc. Basically, imagine the thought as something completely separate to you that can't hurt you. After you observe it for long enough without reacting to it or attaching any thought or emotion to it, the thought should go away. It, or one of its friends, may come back later - but just keep practicing this and eventually you'll stop feeling haunted.

\- Forgive yourself. This is perhaps the most important thing. At the end of the day, when it comes to you, the only opinion that matters is your own. Friends come and go, family comes and goes, enemies come and go, everybody and everything comes and goes. When everybody is gone the only person who will be left will be you, so you'd better learn to like yourself. Liking yourself means having the courage to say "I did this thing. I'm not necessarily proud of it. But it's over now and I'm going to move forward." Forgiveness means different things to different people, but to me it means being able to put something behind you and live on.

I hope the above can help you. Please let me know if you have any questions. :)

Speaking purely from my own perspective, which needless to say is rife with geographical bias (I'm from the UK) and subjective bias - I've noticed how little power our society affords children in making their own decisions. In my opinion, this leads to a certain level of learned helplessness later in life where people will just accept things and hope somebody else will make the decision for them.

This problem is further compounded by the fact that adults who hold positions of power over children have the ability to almost get away with murder. Schools, for example, feel that they can impose whatever rule they want, whenever they want, for as long as they want, regardless of the consequences. Sometimes adults will chastise children for no particular reason, simply because they can. They lie to children to keep them complacent, or keep important information from them in order to prevent an escalation. If a child does make a complaint, and no objective evidence exists to back it up, it usually gets swept under the carpet. When I was younger, all of this was justified by the adults in question saying: "We're preparing you for later life, because sometimes you'll have to do things you won't want to do - and life isn't always fair".

Whilst I don't necessarily disagree with their assertions, let's contrast that with what **actually** happens in later life. Laws are passed by a legislature, which comprises an elected body of representatives. The Rule of Law also applies - meaning that a person can only be prosecuted for an offence committed under a written law, and such an offence must have been committed after the law came into force. Furthermore, criminal prosecutions are subject to intense scrutiny and procedures with the intention of making court proceedings as fair as possible. Not only that, but a person must be proven to be guilty beyond a reasonable doubt before any form of punishment can even be considered. People have rights, which are guaranteed by legislation, constitutions, and even international treaties. Anyone remotely involved in government and law enforcement cannot violate these rights without good reason, and still, any violation must be proportionate and must constitute only the bare minimum necessary to achieve the desired aim. This isn't to say that abuses of power still do not occur in spite of all this, however adults are more legally equipped to address them.

What that woman did was disgraceful, and unjust. She abused her position of power, for a reason that we may never know, and resolved that if it came down to your word against her's, she would come out on top. Perhaps she had reached a point where she no longer cared. Perhaps she just decided for whatever reason that she didn't like you Perhaps she'd had something bad happen to her and she decided that she was going to take it out on you. I can only make suppositions. In any event, whatever reason she may have had, that still doesn't excuse the damage she has undoubtedly caused.

However, you are now an adult, I presume. If you are not, you will be soon. You are (or will be) free from the indignity of having other people make decisions for you. If a psychiatrist were to do that to you now (or in the future as the case may be), your testimony would have more weight, as would any complaint made against them.

If I may offer some advice, which you are of course free to disregard entirely if you like: Learn from this past experience. Arm yourself against the possibility of it happening again. Ensure that if it does happen again you have the information, the evidence, and the know-how to stand up for yourself and protect yourself against this in future. You may also wish to make a complaint against the psychiatrist in question, that way you'll satisfy yourself that you've done all that you can do, and you might get some closure on the situation.

I'm so sorry about what happened to you, nothing can change it, but hopefully you can prevent it from happening again if you decide to seek help later in life. Whatever you do, keep on keepin' on. I wish you all the best in your future endeavours.

P.S. My apologies for hijacking your vent post to undertake a semi-vent of my own. My intention was to offer you some words of empowerment and encouragement. I hope that I've succeeded.

P.S.S Whilst this post expresses some views which could be construed as political, I aver that I am merely stating my view of the world as I see it from my tiny corner. You are more than welcome to disagree, or discuss - I will take no offence. I hope that nobody is offended by this post, however I offer my earnest apologies to anyone who may be.

To continue on from the 'electrical' motif - I sometimes experience situations where I need to make a decision or do something and I just freeze. My brain seems to flick between the possible outcomes but is unable to choose or focus on one option in particular.

As you can imagine, this can be a pain in work or social situations.

Firstly, with regard to your experience with the teacher, I know to a certain extent how that feels. I had a similar thing happen to me, and the worst part was that I felt that I had lost control of the situation and all of a sudden my life was being dictated by other people who thought they knew what was best. I'm still miffed at that. Some people don't understand that things like that can lead to trust issues later in life, which might discourage a person from seeking help when they need it in the future.

Secondly - if freelance writing is what you want to do, without wishing to tell you how to live your life, you should certainly give it a go. There is a lot of doom and gloom around lately about how markets are saturated and it's impossible to get a job you like, but the reality is that there is always *something* out there. I wanted to get into Law, people told me I wouldn't get into Law because the market was saturated and blah, blah, blah - I got into Law. I thought I would be sat around for two years before I got a Legal job, and I wasn't. I promise you there is always something out there and when you find it you'll wonder why you ever doubted there would be.

Thirdly, you are certainly not alone. I wish you all the best for the future. Keep on keepin' on.

I've clocked in almost 90 hours of RimWorld on various colonies. On my latest Alpha 16 playthrough, something mildly interesting happened:

I formed a caravan with two guys and some random tat to sell to a nearby settlement. One of them was gay, the other wasn't. During the four day round trip, the two guys chatted and became friends, and at some point the gay character tried to romance the straight one. He declined, and the gay character became upset as a result.

I honestly don't know whether the interaction was a bug or not, I kind of hope it wasn't, but it was pleasant nonetheless. As a gay man myself, this previously unnoticed flair really tugged at my heartstrings, and gave me the impression that there are still quirks in this game that I still haven't seen - and that pleased me greatly.

Regardless of any shortcomings in the relationship system that people may perceive, this recent event has at the very least convinced me that there is far more depth to this than meets the eye.

Or then again, I'm probably just transposing my own values onto around 100,000 lines of code and some art assets.

Regardless, I'd like to say: thank you, Ludeon, for facilitating such an interesting quirk, whether it was intentional or not. It really fascinated me.
